presidentialSuccession.name: Daniel Ortega
presidentialSuccession.notes: Re-elected repeatedly; co-presidency with Rosario Murillo from 2025 constitutional change.

supremeCourt.name: Corte Suprema de Justicia (CSJ)
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Magistrates elected by the National Assembly.
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: The judiciary has been consolidated under FSLN control. In 2009 the CSJ Constitutional Chamber set aside the constitutional ban on consecutive presidential re-election, enabling Ortega’s continued rule; later codified by constitutional reform (2014).
supremeCourt.stillServing: The court remains under FSLN control; after the 2009 ruling and 2014 constitutional reform there is no independent bloc, and the judiciary has been central to Ortega and Murillo's consolidation of power. Exact 2026 roster not individually itemised here.

courtHistory.event: Under the Somoza dynasty the judiciary was subordinated to the regime; the 1979 Sandinista revolution and 1987 Constitution rebuilt the court.
Post-revolution court under Chamorro; magistrates elected by the National Assembly.
The Alemán–Ortega pact ('El Pacto') divided control of the CSJ and other state bodies between the PLC and the FSLN by quota, politicising judicial appointments.
The CSJ Constitutional Chamber set aside the constitutional ban on consecutive presidential re-election, clearing the way for Ortega's continued rule.
Constitutional reform codified indefinite presidential re-election and further entrenched FSLN control of the judiciary.

benchControl.note: The Alemán–Ortega pact's January 2000 constitutional reform expanded the CSJ from 12 to 16 magistrates, split by quota between the PLC and the FSLN — the FSLN held a share of the bench while in opposition. Pre-2000 composition is not itemized here.

With Ortega back in office the FSLN's pact-era quota anchored growing control; in October 2009 a Constitutional Chamber session convened with FSLN-appointed magistrates set aside the ban on consecutive presidential re-election.

Decree 3-2010 kept pro-government magistrates in office after their terms expired (Freedom House); the IACHR's 2021 report describes a judiciary subordinated to the executive, with no independent bloc remaining on the CSJ.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: The CSJ (16 magistrates) is FSLN-aligned; individual members are not itemized here.

fspParties.note: The FSLN is Nicaragua's FSP founding member.

legislativeControl.seats: The FSLN lost power in 1990 (Chamorro/UNO) and sat in opposition through the Alemán and Bolaños governments (though it remained the second bloc).
Ortega returned to the presidency in 2007; the FSLN was the largest bloc and governed with allied votes before winning an outright majority in 2011.
FSLN majority from 2012, a supermajority from 2016 (roughly 70–75 of 90 elected seats).
legislativeControl.notes: The 2016 and 2021 elections were widely condemned as neither free nor fair — leading opposition figures were barred or jailed before the 2021 vote — so the supermajority is real but the elections' legitimacy is disputed.

government.note: Reported result of an election the OAS, EU and US said was neither free nor fair: authorities had jailed or forced into exile the leading opposition candidates (seven presidential aspirants disqualified or arrested) and the main opposition coalitions were barred or boycotted. The parties that did run alongside the FSLN are widely described as collaborationist. The 90 elected seats shown exclude the two ex-officio seats (outgoing president and presidential runner-up). ALBA-TCP, by contrast, welcomed the result.

The FSLN jumped to 63 of 92 seats (90 elected plus two ex-officio) — its first supermajority, above the two-thirds needed to amend the constitution, later used for the 2014 reform abolishing presidential term limits. The election itself was contested: the constitution then barred consecutive re-election, and Ortega's candidacy rested on a 2009 ruling by the FSLN-aligned Supreme Court's constitutional chamber setting the ban aside. Runner-up Fabio Gadea (PLI) rejected the results as fraudulent, and EU and OAS observer missions reported serious irregularities and a lack of transparency; the government and its allies maintained the vote was valid.
